To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GraphLab, Apache Giraff and Apache Flink are well suited for large networks and NetworKit for small ones.

(i) GraphLab and Apache Flink are the fastest frameworks in our experiments, (ii) Apache Giraph and Giraph++ are the most scalable, (iii) the shared-memory parallel NetworKit outperforms all other implementations for networks that fit in memory, and (iv) the best framework is Apache Giraph for the analysis of large networks.
the best performing frameworks for distributed graph processing are GraphLab and Apache Flink for small graphs and Apache Giraph for large graphs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) How do the performance and scalability of distributed frameworks compare to a shared-memory parallel framework?
the practical use of distributed computing for network analysis and the evaluation of the state-of-the-art in this field.
the question of whether distributed computing is a viable alternative to shared-memory parallel computing for network analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best framework depends on the task at hand.
there is no single best framework for all tasks, but rather a combination of different approaches is needed to achieve the best performance for a given task and data size.
the best framework depends on the problem, the data and the hardware.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best choice is to use NetworKit for small networks, Apache Giraph for medium-sized ones and GraphLab for the largest.
the distributed systems are useful for large networks, whereas shared memory systems are more efficient for small and medium networks.
for the studied problems, a cluster of eight machines is not required to analyze networks of 2 billion edges and the shared memory parallel approach is still superior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single framework that outperforms the rest in all cases.
the distributed computing frameworks are not yet mature enough to be used as general-purpose tools for large-scale complex networks.
, in practice, the choice of the framework depends on the data volume and the algorithm.
